1	# 3.1 The Periodic Table and chemical periodicity
2	
3	*nam-8224-nsscas-2026. Offline study notes, rendered from the approved content units on 2026-10-22. Everything here is also what the flashcards are built from.*
4	
5	---
6	
7	## The Periodic Table and chemical periodicity — 3.1.1
8	
9	### Ionisation energy specifies particles and states
10	
11	First ionisation energy is the energy required to remove one electron from each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms, forming one mole of gaseous singly positive ions. The equation is X(g) → X+(g) + e−. “Gaseous” excludes energy changes involved in melting, vaporising or dissolving a sample. “First” specifies removal from a neutral atom rather than from an ion that has already lost electrons.
12	
13	Ionisation requires an energy input to overcome the attraction between the nucleus and the electron. A molar ionisation energy is positive and is commonly quoted in kJ mol⁻¹. It is not the energy released when an atom gains an electron, and it is not a measure of the mass of the electron. The electron symbol accounts for the negative charge removed; the gaseous atom becomes a 1+ ion.
14	
15	For a supplied first ionisation energy of 600 kJ mol⁻¹, ionising 0.0200 mol of separate gaseous atoms requires 12.0 kJ under the stated ideal amount basis. The calculation is energy = amount × molar ionisation energy. The example does not include energy to obtain those gaseous atoms from a solid sample. Such additional steps would need their own data.
16	
17	Second ionisation instead removes an electron from each gaseous singly positive ion: X+(g) → X2+(g) + e−. Successive values describe different starting particles. A large jump after a given number of removals can indicate that further removal reaches an inner shell. When interpreting a series, count which electron is being removed before assigning the jump. The definition, equation and amount basis make ionisation data usable for comparing elements and inferring their outer-electron arrangements.
18	
19	### Explaining attraction rather than quoting a trend
20	
21	An electron is attracted to the positive nucleus. For comparable electronic arrangements, a larger nuclear charge tends to hold it more strongly and raises the energy needed to remove it. The comparison must also account for the electron's distance and shielding. More protons do not by themselves prove that an atom has the larger ionisation energy.
22	
23	An outer electron farther from the nucleus is generally less strongly attracted. Inner electrons shield it from part of the nuclear attraction, reducing the effective pull it experiences. Down a group, added shells make outer electrons more distant and increase shielding. These effects can outweigh the increase in proton number, explaining why removal becomes easier even though the nucleus has greater charge.
24	
25	Across a period, electrons are added to the same main shell while nuclear charge increases. Inner-shell shielding changes relatively little, so the outer electrons tend to feel a stronger effective attraction. This provides a general reason for a rise in first ionisation energy. Shell and subshell energies also matter to the detailed pattern; use the scope of the question rather than turning the broad trend into a strict step-by-step rule.
26	
27	For an explanation, name the particles and connect cause to consequence: greater shielding and distance reduce attraction between nucleus and outer electron, so less energy is needed for removal. Merely saying that an atom has more electrons leaves out their location and effect. Likewise, “it has a bigger nucleus” does not specify nuclear charge. Use the electron arrangement developed in Topic 1.2 to decide which electrons shield and which electron is removed. Keep the comparison tied to gaseous atoms for first ionisation, not to the size of a solid metal sample.
28	
29	### Radius and electronegativity across Period 3
30	
31	Across Period 3, nuclear charge increases while electrons enter the third main shell. Comparable atomic radii generally decrease because inner-shell shielding changes relatively little and effective attraction strengthens. The added electrons do not force a general expansion: increased positive charge draws the outer distribution closer to the nucleus. Use the same radius definition when comparing measurements; a van der Waals radius is not directly interchangeable with a covalent radius.
32	
33	Ionic radii need separate comparisons. Na+, Mg2+ and Al3+ each contain ten electrons. Their radii decrease in that order because the same electron population experiences increasing nuclear charge. These cations are smaller than their parent atoms, with the third shell emptied in these examples. In contrast, P3−, S2− and Cl− each have eighteen electrons and retain a third shell. Within that sequence, increasing nuclear charge again contracts the electron cloud, so radius decreases from P3− to Cl−.
34	
35	Do not join the two ion sequences into one smooth decreasing line across the period. Moving from small cations to larger anions changes the shell population and ionic charge. An anion is generally larger than its parent atom because adding electrons increases electron repulsion without adding protons. State the ions being compared rather than treating “ionic radius” as a unique value for an element without a charge.
36	
37	Electronegativity is the ability of an atom in a bond to attract the shared electron pair. It generally increases from sodium towards chlorine as atomic size falls and effective nuclear attraction rises. Argon is not assigned an ordinary value merely by extending the line, because the usual comparison concerns bonded atoms. These ideas link the Period 3 trend to the bond polarity explained in Topic 1.3.
38	
39	### The general first-ionisation trend
40	
41	From sodium towards argon, first ionisation energy generally rises. Sodium has a relatively easily removed outer electron, while argon's outer electrons are held much more strongly. The general explanation is increasing nuclear charge across the period, electrons entering the same main shell and a reduction in atomic radius. Inner shielding does not increase enough to cancel the extra positive charge.
42	
43	Removing an electron from the right-hand end therefore generally requires more energy. State that the comparison concerns separate gaseous atoms and the first electron removed. Conductivity, melting point and chemical reactivity describe different properties and do not substitute for the nuclear-attraction explanation.
44	
45	The word “general” matters. Experimental first ionisation energies do not form a perfectly smooth increasing series. Do not erase a local decrease in supplied data simply to preserve a memorised arrow across the table. Describe the broad pattern and any stated departure accurately, while keeping the explanation at the required level. The common-shell, rising-nuclear-charge account explains the overall trend; it does not assert that electronic details have no influence.
46	
47	When using a table, identify the start and end of the period and the units before comparing. A larger positive value means more energy is required per mole for the defined removal, not a greater amount of energy released. An unknown with a much lower first value than its neighbours may have a more weakly held outer electron, but identity normally needs additional evidence. Successive ionisation data can provide a different clue about how many outer electrons are removed before an inner shell is reached. These comparisons use the same definition, keeping atom, ion and bulk-property evidence separate.
48	
49	### Melting and conduction depend on structure
50	
51	Period 3 changes from metallic structures through a giant covalent network to molecular and monatomic substances. Sodium, magnesium and aluminium have positive metal centres attracted to delocalised electrons. Their metallic bonds must be overcome during melting, and their mobile electrons carry current in the solid. Melting points generally rise across these three as metal-ion charge and the supply of delocalised electrons increase, with size also affecting attraction.
52	
53	Silicon has a giant covalent network. Melting requires disruption of strong covalent bonding throughout the extended structure, giving a high melting point. It is a semiconductor rather than an ordinary good metallic conductor. Its conductivity depends on the availability of mobile carriers and the material's state; a giant structure alone is not enough to classify electrical behaviour.
54	
55	White phosphorus contains P4 molecules, sulphur contains S8 molecules and chlorine contains Cl2 molecules in their familiar elemental forms. Melting these molecular solids overcomes intermolecular attractions rather than breaking their covalent molecules apart. Their melting points are much lower than silicon's. Sulphur's larger molecular electron population gives stronger dispersion attractions than the small P4 or Cl2 comparison would suggest from position alone. Argon is monatomic and has weak dispersion attractions between atoms, giving a very low melting point.
56	
57	These non-metal molecular and atomic substances lack the mobile charged particles needed for ordinary electrical conduction. Do not explain their low melting points by calling their internal covalent bonds weak. Nor should the high melting point of silicon be used to infer that it conducts as well as aluminium. Identify structure, the interactions disrupted on melting, and the available charge carriers separately. This applies Topic 1.3's structure–property reasoning to a whole period rather than treating each numerical property as an isolated fact.
58	
59	---
60	
61	## The Periodic Table and chemical periodicity — 3.1.2
62	
63	### Comparing atoms and ions down a group
64	
65	Down Group 2 or Group 17, atoms have additional occupied main shells. Their outer electrons lie farther from the nucleus, and inner electrons provide more shielding. Atomic radius therefore generally increases despite the larger nuclear charge. A valid explanation includes both the rising proton number and why distance and shielding dominate its effect on the outer region.
66	
67	Comparable ions also become larger down these groups. In Group 2 compare the 2+ cations, such as Mg2+ and Ca2+. In Group 17 compare the 1− anions, such as F−, Cl− and Br−. The lower member has more occupied shells. Do not mix a neutral atom of one element with an ion of another and describe the result as the group ionic-radius trend.
68	
69	Electronegativity generally decreases down each group. The shared electron pair in a bond is farther from the nucleus and experiences greater shielding, so the attraction for it is reduced. Increased nuclear charge alone would suggest stronger attraction, but omits the larger electron structure. This is why a statement that “more protons means higher electronegativity” needs a controlled comparison rather than being applied without considering shell number.
70	
71	For an unfamiliar Group 17 member below chlorine, a reasonable prediction is a larger atom and halide ion, with lower electronegativity than chlorine. This prediction uses relative position, not an invented numerical radius. If a question supplies measured radii, confirm that they refer to the same charge and radius convention. Group 2 metal and Group 17 non-metal chemistry differ, but the distance-and-shielding argument can be applied to both when the compared quantities are defined consistently. Topics 3.2 and 3.4 develop the chemical consequences.
72	
73	### Ionisation down Groups 2 and 17
74	
75	First ionisation energy generally decreases down Group 2 and down Group 17. The removed electron occupies an outer shell at greater average distance from the nucleus. More inner electrons shield it. Less energy is needed to overcome the effective attraction, even though the lower element contains more protons.
76	
77	For a Group 2 comparison, the outer electrons retain the same general valence pattern while main shell number increases. Removing the first electron from a lower gaseous atom is therefore easier in the broad trend. For halogen atoms, the outer-shell arrangement also repeats down the group, and the added shells similarly reduce the energy needed for first removal. This statement concerns ionisation, not the halogens' tendency to gain an electron in a separate reaction.
78	
79	Use a full chain in an explanation: added shells give greater radius and shielding; the removed electron experiences weaker effective attraction; first ionisation energy decreases. A statement that lower atoms have “more shielding” without identifying the inner electrons or the nucleus–electron attraction is incomplete reasoning. Conversely, a statement about increased proton number alone predicts the wrong general direction for this comparison.
80	
81	If supplied data ask for a comparison between two different groups as well as two periods, do not apply a one-dimensional trend blindly. Identify shell number, nuclear charge and the electron being removed. Group trends are most directly useful when comparing members of the same group. In an unknown-element problem, combine the general ionisation trend with evidence about ion charge, outer electrons or chemical reactions before assigning a position. This avoids treating one energy value as a unique fingerprint independent of the rest of the periodic pattern.
82	
83	---
84	
85	## The Periodic Table and chemical periodicity — 3.1.3
86	
87	### Specified reactions with oxygen, chlorine and water
88	
89	Write the intended product before balancing a Period 3 combination reaction. For the specified oxides, 4Na(s) + O2(g) → 2Na2O(s), 2Mg(s) + O2(g) → 2MgO(s), and 4Al(s) + 3O2(g) → 2Al2O3(s). Magnesium burns with a bright white light. Aluminium's protective surface oxide can slow visible reaction of bulk metal; the equation describes the oxide-forming change rather than the rate of an untreated object.
90	
91	For phosphorus(V) oxide, P4(s) + 5O2(g) → P4O10(s). Sulphur burns mainly to sulphur dioxide: S(s) + O2(g) → SO2(g), with a blue flame. Sulphur trioxide is formed by further oxidation, 2SO2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2SO3(g), using suitable catalytic operating settings. Do not treat that last equilibrium step as proof that ordinary sulphur combustion gives pure SO3 directly.
92	
93	With chlorine, 2Na(s) + Cl2(g) → 2NaCl(s) and Mg(s) + Cl2(g) → MgCl2(s). The syllabus represents aluminium chloride as Al2Cl6: 2Al(s) + 3Cl2(g) → Al2Cl6 in the molecular dimer description. State the relevant physical form if a problem requires its state symbol rather than assuming its molecular form is independent of temperature. Silicon gives SiCl4(l) from Si(s) + 2Cl2(g), and phosphorus in excess chlorine gives PCl5: P4(s) + 10Cl2(g) → 4PCl5(s).
94	
95	Sodium reacts readily with cold water: 2Na(s) + 2H2O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H2(g). Magnesium reacts only slowly with cold water, forming Mg(OH)2 and hydrogen, but heated magnesium reacts with steam: Mg(s) + H2O(g) → MgO(s) + H2(g). The water state changes both rate and the stated solid product. These equations connect the observations with atom balance; they are not interchangeable descriptions of one experiment.
96	
97	### Oxidation numbers follow valence-electron accounting
98	
99	Use oxygen as −2 in these oxides and chlorine as −1 in the specified chlorides. Charge balance then assigns the other element's oxidation number. Na2O gives sodium +1, MgO gives magnesium +2 and Al2O3 gives aluminium +3. In SiO2, silicon is +4; in P4O10, phosphorus is +5. Sulphur is +4 in SO2 but +6 in SO3, so distinguish a particular oxide from the highest oxide in the comparison.
100	
101	For the specified highest oxides from sodium through sulphur, the maximum positive numbers rise +1, +2, +3, +4, +5 and +6. They do not rise and then fall merely because the elements change from metals to non-metals. The increasing outer-electron count provides the formal valence accounting behind this sequence. It is a maximum-state trend for a named series, not a statement that a particular element has one oxidation number in all compounds.
102	
103	The chlorides NaCl, MgCl2, Al2Cl6, SiCl4 and PCl5 give +1, +2, +3, +4 and +5 respectively. For Al2Cl6, two aluminium atoms together balance six chlorines at −1, so each aluminium is +3. Do not give one aluminium a +6 value by overlooking the subscript two.
104	
105	Formal oxidation number does not establish bonding type. Silicon +4 in SiCl4 does not mean there are separate Si4+ and Cl− ions inside a liquid molecule. Nor does phosphorus +5 require P5+ ions. Link the numbers to the written composition, then use physical and chemical evidence for structure. As a check on an incorrect maximum-oxide sequence, calculate phosphorus in P4O10 and sulphur in SO3 explicitly; their +5 and +6 values test whether a proposed falling trend can be correct.
106	
107	### Oxides in contact with water
108	
109	Sodium oxide reacts with water to give sodium hydroxide: Na2O(s) + H2O(l) → 2NaOH(aq). The solution is alkaline. Magnesium oxide reacts much less readily and forms sparingly soluble magnesium hydroxide: MgO(s) + H2O(l) → Mg(OH)2(s). The modest dissolved hydroxide amount can still give an alkaline mixture. State both the chemical product and the observed extent rather than assuming that both oxides dissolve readily.
110	
111	Aluminium oxide does not react appreciably with water in this ordinary comparison, and silicon dioxide also remains essentially unchanged. This lack of reaction does not by itself decide acid/base character. Aluminium oxide is amphoteric, while silicon dioxide behaves as an acidic oxide in reaction with strong alkali under suitable heating. A water test and an acid/base reaction test answer different questions.
112	
113	Phosphorus(V) oxide reacts to form phosphoric(V) acid: P4O10(s) + 6H2O(l) → 4H3PO4(aq). Sulphur trioxide reacts with water to form sulphuric acid: SO3 + H2O(l) → H2SO4(aq), with a large heat release. Sulphur dioxide dissolves to give an acidic solution; the school representation SO2(g) + H2O(l) ⇌ H2SO3(aq) describes that aqueous acid system. Its reverse direction and changing concentrations matter, so it is not a claim that the liquid contains only one isolated molecular species.
114	
115	Across the selected oxides, strongly basic behaviour gives way through amphoteric aluminium oxide to acidic non-metal oxides. Acidic-oxide character does not imply ready dissolution in water: SiO2 is an acidic oxide that does not simply form an acid solution with water, so reaction evidence must be interpreted separately from solubility. Use equations and named observations together to explain what each oxide does.
116	
117	### Basic, acidic and amphoteric behaviour
118	
119	Basic oxides react with acids to form a salt and water. For example, MgO(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl2(aq) + H2O(l). Magnesium hydroxide behaves similarly: Mg(OH)2(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl2(aq) + 2H2O(l). Sodium hydroxide neutralises an acid through H+(aq) + OH−(aq) → H2O(l). Its high water solubility is a separate property from its ability to accept protons.
120	
121	Aluminium oxide and aluminium hydroxide are amphoteric: they react with acids and with strong alkali such as sodium hydroxide. In acid, Al2O3(s) + 6H+(aq) → 2Al3+(aq) + 3H2O(l). In aqueous alkali, Al2O3(s) + 2OH−(aq) + 3H2O(l) → 2[Al(OH)4]−(aq). The hydroxide analogues are Al(OH)3(s) + 3H+(aq) → Al3+(aq) + 3H2O(l), and Al(OH)3(s) + OH−(aq) → [Al(OH)4]−(aq).
122	
123	The hydroxoaluminate notation states the aqueous alkaline product. If a problem specifies a different heated or dehydrated product form, balance the equation for that stated form instead. Do not mix an aqueous complex product and an anhydrous salt representation without accounting for water. Sodium ions can be omitted as spectators in the net ionic version.
124	
125	An acidic oxide reacts with alkali. For example, SO3 + 2NaOH(aq) → Na2SO4(aq) + H2O(l), and heated SiO2(s) + 2NaOH → Na2SiO3 + H2O. The latter needs suitable strong-alkali heating and is not a claim of rapid reaction with a dilute cold solution. For phosphorus(V) oxide, full neutralisation gives P4O10 + 12NaOH → 4Na3PO4 + 6H2O; the stated amount of base determines the degree of neutralisation. Explain amphoterism by both acid and alkali reactions, rather than merely saying that a substance has an intermediate pH.
126	
127	### Chlorides with water: dissolving or reacting
128	
129	Sodium chloride dissolves by separating and hydrating its ions. It does not undergo substantial acid-producing hydrolysis, so a simple aqueous NaCl solution is approximately neutral. Magnesium chloride also supplies hydrated ions and is commonly described as weakly acidic rather than as violently hydrolysing. The magnesium cation's interaction with surrounding water is different from sodium's.
130	
131	Aluminium chloride gives a distinctly acidic aqueous solution. Although the anhydrous chloride has covalent character and the syllabus uses the Al2Cl6 dimer description, water forms hydrated aluminium ions. A hydrated Al3+ ion strongly polarises O–H bonds in attached water, allowing proton transfer to surrounding water. A useful first-stage representation is [Al(H2O)6]3+(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ [Al(H2O)5OH]2+(aq) + H3O+(aq). The increased H3O+ concentration explains acidity. Do not assume that simply adding much water precipitates all aluminium as Al(OH)3.
132	
133	Silicon tetrachloride reacts strongly with water: SiCl4(l) + 2H2O(l) → SiO2(s) + 4HCl(aq). The white solid is often hydrated silica in practice, and hydrogen chloride produces acidic fumes in moist air. The simplified equation accounts for the main composition without representing the real solid as a single dissolved ion.
134	
135	With excess water, PCl5(s) + 4H2O(l) → H3PO4(aq) + 5HCl(aq). With limited water other intermediate products can be retained, so the excess-water qualification belongs to this equation. The gaseous molecular description of PCl5 must also be distinguished from its ionic solid structure when interpreting physical data. Across these examples, soluble ionic chlorides and hydrolysing covalent chlorides can both produce conducting solutions; the solution products, rather than the original bonding alone, carry charge. Distinguish dissolution from hydrolysis by whether a chemical reaction with water produces new species such as acid.
136	
137	### Interpreting the pattern through bonding
138	
139	Sodium and magnesium are electropositive metals. Their large electronegativity differences from oxygen or chlorine favour ionic descriptions for the usual oxides and chlorides. Across Period 3, electronegativity generally increases. The difference from oxygen or chlorine becomes smaller, and shared-electron covalent descriptions become more important. Aluminium sits in a useful intermediate position: its oxide is commonly treated as an ionic lattice with appreciable covalent character, while its anhydrous chloride has a strongly covalent description.
140	
141	Silicon dioxide is a giant covalent network, whereas SiCl4 is molecular. Both contain silicon formally at +4, so oxidation number alone does not decide whether the compound is molecular, giant or ionic. The partners, geometry and bonding arrangement matter. Phosphorus and sulphur oxides and their reactions with water provide further examples of covalent non-metal chemistry.
142	
143	The acid/base trend is related but needs its own evidence. Basic Na2O and MgO react with acids; Al2O3 reacts with acid and alkali; selected non-metal oxides react with alkali and often form acidic solutions with water. SiO2 requires particular care because its strong network resists ordinary water reaction despite its acidic-oxide behaviour. A decreasing water-reaction rate is not the same as a decreasing tendency to act as an acid towards alkali.
144	
145	When interpreting a supplied table, connect a property to the interaction that explains it. A low boiling point can support a molecular structure with weak intermolecular forces. A high melting point may instead indicate an ionic lattice or a covalent network, which further evidence must distinguish. Acidity after adding water describes the products of that interaction, not a direct measurement of the original compound's bond type. Use several linked observations to support the periodic interpretation.
146	
147	### Inferring bonding from a set of observations
148	
149	Bonding inference is an argument from evidence rather than a name attached to one property. A chloride that has a high melting point, does not conduct as a solid and conducts when molten is consistent with an ionic lattice. Fixed ions explain the solid's lack of conduction, and mobile ions explain the melt. The high melting point reflects strong lattice attractions.
150	
151	A volatile chloride with a low boiling point and poor electrical conduction as a pure liquid is consistent with discrete molecules. Weak intermolecular attractions allow easy separation of the molecules. Its internal covalent bonds need not be weak. If adding water produces an acidic conducting solution, the new solution may contain ions formed by hydrolysis; that does not retrospectively prove the original liquid was ionic.
152	
153	A high-melting oxide that is a poor ordinary conductor can be a giant covalent network such as SiO2. High melting point alone cannot distinguish it from MgO. Look for molten conduction, reaction behaviour or other stated evidence before choosing a structure. Likewise, a semiconducting element should not be treated as a typical metal merely because a small current can pass.
154	
155	Consider two invented observations: chloride A melts at a high temperature and conducts only after melting; chloride B is a volatile nonconducting liquid that forms acid with water. Ionic A and molecular B are supported interpretations, but the measurements do not identify their elements uniquely. Use the Period 3 possibilities and any additional composition data to narrow identity. A good answer quotes the discriminating observation, supplies the particle model and states any remaining ambiguity. This is the same structure–property reasoning as Topic 1.3, now used to make a deduction from unfamiliar chloride and oxide evidence.
156	
157	---
158	
159	## The Periodic Table and chemical periodicity — 3.1.4
160	
161	### Making a controlled group prediction
162	
163	An element's group provides a useful first prediction because main-group members share a related outer-electron arrangement. Group 2 atoms have two outer electrons and commonly form 2+ ions. Group 17 atoms have seven outer electrons and commonly form 1− halide ions in ionic salts. Group similarity predicts a family of behaviour, not identical numerical properties.
164	
165	Use a known neighbour as a comparison. For a Group 2 element below magnesium, larger radius and greater shielding make removal of outer electrons easier in the general trend. Stronger reaction with water may therefore be expected when comparing otherwise suitable samples. It is not necessary to invent an exact time or gas-production rate. Surface oxide, temperature and physical form can affect observations, so state the qualitative basis of the prediction.
166	
167	For a Group 17 element below chlorine, predict larger atoms and halide ions, and lower electronegativity. Its elemental form remains diatomic in the ordinary halogen pattern. Avoid transferring the metal's electron-loss reactivity explanation directly to a halogen's electron-gain chemistry. The shared periodic vocabulary of charge, radius and shielding does not make their chemical roles the same.
168	
169	When asked to suggest a property of an unfamiliar element, start with the stated group and the relevant comparison. Link the predicted property to an outer-electron or structural reason. Distinguish a direct group feature, such as typical ion charge, from a down-group tendency, such as changing radius. If the group is not given, use composition, ionisation or reaction data first to infer it. An uncertain position should give a conditional prediction rather than a falsely certain identity. The following section combines those clues to identify an unknown.
170	
171	### Combining clues to identify an unknown
172	
173	An unknown element is best identified from several independent clues. Electrical conduction and metallic appearance may indicate a metal but do not distinguish sodium, magnesium and aluminium. A typical ion charge can narrow the group. A known period or occupied-shell count then narrows the position further. Check that the proposed identity accounts for the chemical reactions as well as the physical evidence.
174	
175	For an original example, an unknown is in Period 3, conducts as a solid, forms a common 2+ ion and gives a basic oxide. These clues together support magnesium. A metal below it in the same group would have more occupied shells and a larger atom, so it would not satisfy the Period 3 clue. A common 3+ ion would instead require a different candidate and acid/base evidence would need checking.
176	
177	Successive ionisation data can provide another route. A large jump after the second electron has been removed suggests two relatively accessible outer electrons before reaching a more tightly held inner shell. Combined with a Period 3 location and metallic behaviour, that again supports Group 2 magnesium. The jump is evidence about electronic arrangement, not an instruction to use the largest raw number as a group label.
178	
179	For a nonconducting Period 3 substance with a very high melting point, a giant covalent description suggests silicon rather than the simple molecular elements. If its chloride is a volatile liquid that hydrolyses, that strengthens the identification. Each extra clue should discriminate between candidates. Where the evidence leaves two plausible choices, name the uncertainty and state what further observation would decide. This is a chemical deduction: properties and electron arrangement must agree, rather than a guess from one familiar reaction.

# 3.1 The Periodic Table and chemical periodicity

*nam-8224-nsscas-2026. Offline study notes, rendered from the approved content units on 2026-10-22. Everything here is also what the flashcards are built from.*

---

## The Periodic Table and chemical periodicity — 3.1.1

### Ionisation energy specifies particles and states

First ionisation energy is the energy required to remove one electron from each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms, forming one mole of gaseous singly positive ions. The equation is X(g) → X+(g) + e−. “Gaseous” excludes energy changes involved in melting, vaporising or dissolving a sample. “First” specifies removal from a neutral atom rather than from an ion that has already lost electrons.

Ionisation requires an energy input to overcome the attraction between the nucleus and the electron. A molar ionisation energy is positive and is commonly quoted in kJ mol⁻¹. It is not the energy released when an atom gains an electron, and it is not a measure of the mass of the electron. The electron symbol accounts for the negative charge removed; the gaseous atom becomes a 1+ ion.

For a supplied first ionisation energy of 600 kJ mol⁻¹, ionising 0.0200 mol of separate gaseous atoms requires 12.0 kJ under the stated ideal amount basis. The calculation is energy = amount × molar ionisation energy. The example does not include energy to obtain those gaseous atoms from a solid sample. Such additional steps would need their own data.

Second ionisation instead removes an electron from each gaseous singly positive ion: X+(g) → X2+(g) + e−. Successive values describe different starting particles. A large jump after a given number of removals can indicate that further removal reaches an inner shell. When interpreting a series, count which electron is being removed before assigning the jump. The definition, equation and amount basis make ionisation data usable for comparing elements and inferring their outer-electron arrangements.

### Explaining attraction rather than quoting a trend

An electron is attracted to the positive nucleus. For comparable electronic arrangements, a larger nuclear charge tends to hold it more strongly and raises the energy needed to remove it. The comparison must also account for the electron's distance and shielding. More protons do not by themselves prove that an atom has the larger ionisation energy.

An outer electron farther from the nucleus is generally less strongly attracted. Inner electrons shield it from part of the nuclear attraction, reducing the effective pull it experiences. Down a group, added shells make outer electrons more distant and increase shielding. These effects can outweigh the increase in proton number, explaining why removal becomes easier even though the nucleus has greater charge.

Across a period, electrons are added to the same main shell while nuclear charge increases. Inner-shell shielding changes relatively little, so the outer electrons tend to feel a stronger effective attraction. This provides a general reason for a rise in first ionisation energy. Shell and subshell energies also matter to the detailed pattern; use the scope of the question rather than turning the broad trend into a strict step-by-step rule.

For an explanation, name the particles and connect cause to consequence: greater shielding and distance reduce attraction between nucleus and outer electron, so less energy is needed for removal. Merely saying that an atom has more electrons leaves out their location and effect. Likewise, “it has a bigger nucleus” does not specify nuclear charge. Use the electron arrangement developed in Topic 1.2 to decide which electrons shield and which electron is removed. Keep the comparison tied to gaseous atoms for first ionisation, not to the size of a solid metal sample.

### Radius and electronegativity across Period 3

Across Period 3, nuclear charge increases while electrons enter the third main shell. Comparable atomic radii generally decrease because inner-shell shielding changes relatively little and effective attraction strengthens. The added electrons do not force a general expansion: increased positive charge draws the outer distribution closer to the nucleus. Use the same radius definition when comparing measurements; a van der Waals radius is not directly interchangeable with a covalent radius.

Ionic radii need separate comparisons. Na+, Mg2+ and Al3+ each contain ten electrons. Their radii decrease in that order because the same electron population experiences increasing nuclear charge. These cations are smaller than their parent atoms, with the third shell emptied in these examples. In contrast, P3−, S2− and Cl− each have eighteen electrons and retain a third shell. Within that sequence, increasing nuclear charge again contracts the electron cloud, so radius decreases from P3− to Cl−.

Do not join the two ion sequences into one smooth decreasing line across the period. Moving from small cations to larger anions changes the shell population and ionic charge. An anion is generally larger than its parent atom because adding electrons increases electron repulsion without adding protons. State the ions being compared rather than treating “ionic radius” as a unique value for an element without a charge.

Electronegativity is the ability of an atom in a bond to attract the shared electron pair. It generally increases from sodium towards chlorine as atomic size falls and effective nuclear attraction rises. Argon is not assigned an ordinary value merely by extending the line, because the usual comparison concerns bonded atoms. These ideas link the Period 3 trend to the bond polarity explained in Topic 1.3.

### The general first-ionisation trend

From sodium towards argon, first ionisation energy generally rises. Sodium has a relatively easily removed outer electron, while argon's outer electrons are held much more strongly. The general explanation is increasing nuclear charge across the period, electrons entering the same main shell and a reduction in atomic radius. Inner shielding does not increase enough to cancel the extra positive charge.

Removing an electron from the right-hand end therefore generally requires more energy. State that the comparison concerns separate gaseous atoms and the first electron removed. Conductivity, melting point and chemical reactivity describe different properties and do not substitute for the nuclear-attraction explanation.

The word “general” matters. Experimental first ionisation energies do not form a perfectly smooth increasing series. Do not erase a local decrease in supplied data simply to preserve a memorised arrow across the table. Describe the broad pattern and any stated departure accurately, while keeping the explanation at the required level. The common-shell, rising-nuclear-charge account explains the overall trend; it does not assert that electronic details have no influence.

When using a table, identify the start and end of the period and the units before comparing. A larger positive value means more energy is required per mole for the defined removal, not a greater amount of energy released. An unknown with a much lower first value than its neighbours may have a more weakly held outer electron, but identity normally needs additional evidence. Successive ionisation data can provide a different clue about how many outer electrons are removed before an inner shell is reached. These comparisons use the same definition, keeping atom, ion and bulk-property evidence separate.

### Melting and conduction depend on structure

Period 3 changes from metallic structures through a giant covalent network to molecular and monatomic substances. Sodium, magnesium and aluminium have positive metal centres attracted to delocalised electrons. Their metallic bonds must be overcome during melting, and their mobile electrons carry current in the solid. Melting points generally rise across these three as metal-ion charge and the supply of delocalised electrons increase, with size also affecting attraction.

Silicon has a giant covalent network. Melting requires disruption of strong covalent bonding throughout the extended structure, giving a high melting point. It is a semiconductor rather than an ordinary good metallic conductor. Its conductivity depends on the availability of mobile carriers and the material's state; a giant structure alone is not enough to classify electrical behaviour.

White phosphorus contains P4 molecules, sulphur contains S8 molecules and chlorine contains Cl2 molecules in their familiar elemental forms. Melting these molecular solids overcomes intermolecular attractions rather than breaking their covalent molecules apart. Their melting points are much lower than silicon's. Sulphur's larger molecular electron population gives stronger dispersion attractions than the small P4 or Cl2 comparison would suggest from position alone. Argon is monatomic and has weak dispersion attractions between atoms, giving a very low melting point.

These non-metal molecular and atomic substances lack the mobile charged particles needed for ordinary electrical conduction. Do not explain their low melting points by calling their internal covalent bonds weak. Nor should the high melting point of silicon be used to infer that it conducts as well as aluminium. Identify structure, the interactions disrupted on melting, and the available charge carriers separately. This applies Topic 1.3's structure–property reasoning to a whole period rather than treating each numerical property as an isolated fact.

---

## The Periodic Table and chemical periodicity — 3.1.2

### Comparing atoms and ions down a group

Down Group 2 or Group 17, atoms have additional occupied main shells. Their outer electrons lie farther from the nucleus, and inner electrons provide more shielding. Atomic radius therefore generally increases despite the larger nuclear charge. A valid explanation includes both the rising proton number and why distance and shielding dominate its effect on the outer region.

Comparable ions also become larger down these groups. In Group 2 compare the 2+ cations, such as Mg2+ and Ca2+. In Group 17 compare the 1− anions, such as F−, Cl− and Br−. The lower member has more occupied shells. Do not mix a neutral atom of one element with an ion of another and describe the result as the group ionic-radius trend.

Electronegativity generally decreases down each group. The shared electron pair in a bond is farther from the nucleus and experiences greater shielding, so the attraction for it is reduced. Increased nuclear charge alone would suggest stronger attraction, but omits the larger electron structure. This is why a statement that “more protons means higher electronegativity” needs a controlled comparison rather than being applied without considering shell number.

For an unfamiliar Group 17 member below chlorine, a reasonable prediction is a larger atom and halide ion, with lower electronegativity than chlorine. This prediction uses relative position, not an invented numerical radius. If a question supplies measured radii, confirm that they refer to the same charge and radius convention. Group 2 metal and Group 17 non-metal chemistry differ, but the distance-and-shielding argument can be applied to both when the compared quantities are defined consistently. Topics 3.2 and 3.4 develop the chemical consequences.

### Ionisation down Groups 2 and 17

First ionisation energy generally decreases down Group 2 and down Group 17. The removed electron occupies an outer shell at greater average distance from the nucleus. More inner electrons shield it. Less energy is needed to overcome the effective attraction, even though the lower element contains more protons.

For a Group 2 comparison, the outer electrons retain the same general valence pattern while main shell number increases. Removing the first electron from a lower gaseous atom is therefore easier in the broad trend. For halogen atoms, the outer-shell arrangement also repeats down the group, and the added shells similarly reduce the energy needed for first removal. This statement concerns ionisation, not the halogens' tendency to gain an electron in a separate reaction.

Use a full chain in an explanation: added shells give greater radius and shielding; the removed electron experiences weaker effective attraction; first ionisation energy decreases. A statement that lower atoms have “more shielding” without identifying the inner electrons or the nucleus–electron attraction is incomplete reasoning. Conversely, a statement about increased proton number alone predicts the wrong general direction for this comparison.

If supplied data ask for a comparison between two different groups as well as two periods, do not apply a one-dimensional trend blindly. Identify shell number, nuclear charge and the electron being removed. Group trends are most directly useful when comparing members of the same group. In an unknown-element problem, combine the general ionisation trend with evidence about ion charge, outer electrons or chemical reactions before assigning a position. This avoids treating one energy value as a unique fingerprint independent of the rest of the periodic pattern.

---

## The Periodic Table and chemical periodicity — 3.1.3

### Specified reactions with oxygen, chlorine and water

Write the intended product before balancing a Period 3 combination reaction. For the specified oxides, 4Na(s) + O2(g) → 2Na2O(s), 2Mg(s) + O2(g) → 2MgO(s), and 4Al(s) + 3O2(g) → 2Al2O3(s). Magnesium burns with a bright white light. Aluminium's protective surface oxide can slow visible reaction of bulk metal; the equation describes the oxide-forming change rather than the rate of an untreated object.

For phosphorus(V) oxide, P4(s) + 5O2(g) → P4O10(s). Sulphur burns mainly to sulphur dioxide: S(s) + O2(g) → SO2(g), with a blue flame. Sulphur trioxide is formed by further oxidation, 2SO2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2SO3(g), using suitable catalytic operating settings. Do not treat that last equilibrium step as proof that ordinary sulphur combustion gives pure SO3 directly.

With chlorine, 2Na(s) + Cl2(g) → 2NaCl(s) and Mg(s) + Cl2(g) → MgCl2(s). The syllabus represents aluminium chloride as Al2Cl6: 2Al(s) + 3Cl2(g) → Al2Cl6 in the molecular dimer description. State the relevant physical form if a problem requires its state symbol rather than assuming its molecular form is independent of temperature. Silicon gives SiCl4(l) from Si(s) + 2Cl2(g), and phosphorus in excess chlorine gives PCl5: P4(s) + 10Cl2(g) → 4PCl5(s).

Sodium reacts readily with cold water: 2Na(s) + 2H2O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H2(g). Magnesium reacts only slowly with cold water, forming Mg(OH)2 and hydrogen, but heated magnesium reacts with steam: Mg(s) + H2O(g) → MgO(s) + H2(g). The water state changes both rate and the stated solid product. These equations connect the observations with atom balance; they are not interchangeable descriptions of one experiment.

### Oxidation numbers follow valence-electron accounting

Use oxygen as −2 in these oxides and chlorine as −1 in the specified chlorides. Charge balance then assigns the other element's oxidation number. Na2O gives sodium +1, MgO gives magnesium +2 and Al2O3 gives aluminium +3. In SiO2, silicon is +4; in P4O10, phosphorus is +5. Sulphur is +4 in SO2 but +6 in SO3, so distinguish a particular oxide from the highest oxide in the comparison.

For the specified highest oxides from sodium through sulphur, the maximum positive numbers rise +1, +2, +3, +4, +5 and +6. They do not rise and then fall merely because the elements change from metals to non-metals. The increasing outer-electron count provides the formal valence accounting behind this sequence. It is a maximum-state trend for a named series, not a statement that a particular element has one oxidation number in all compounds.

The chlorides NaCl, MgCl2, Al2Cl6, SiCl4 and PCl5 give +1, +2, +3, +4 and +5 respectively. For Al2Cl6, two aluminium atoms together balance six chlorines at −1, so each aluminium is +3. Do not give one aluminium a +6 value by overlooking the subscript two.

Formal oxidation number does not establish bonding type. Silicon +4 in SiCl4 does not mean there are separate Si4+ and Cl− ions inside a liquid molecule. Nor does phosphorus +5 require P5+ ions. Link the numbers to the written composition, then use physical and chemical evidence for structure. As a check on an incorrect maximum-oxide sequence, calculate phosphorus in P4O10 and sulphur in SO3 explicitly; their +5 and +6 values test whether a proposed falling trend can be correct.

### Oxides in contact with water

Sodium oxide reacts with water to give sodium hydroxide: Na2O(s) + H2O(l) → 2NaOH(aq). The solution is alkaline. Magnesium oxide reacts much less readily and forms sparingly soluble magnesium hydroxide: MgO(s) + H2O(l) → Mg(OH)2(s). The modest dissolved hydroxide amount can still give an alkaline mixture. State both the chemical product and the observed extent rather than assuming that both oxides dissolve readily.

Aluminium oxide does not react appreciably with water in this ordinary comparison, and silicon dioxide also remains essentially unchanged. This lack of reaction does not by itself decide acid/base character. Aluminium oxide is amphoteric, while silicon dioxide behaves as an acidic oxide in reaction with strong alkali under suitable heating. A water test and an acid/base reaction test answer different questions.

Phosphorus(V) oxide reacts to form phosphoric(V) acid: P4O10(s) + 6H2O(l) → 4H3PO4(aq). Sulphur trioxide reacts with water to form sulphuric acid: SO3 + H2O(l) → H2SO4(aq), with a large heat release. Sulphur dioxide dissolves to give an acidic solution; the school representation SO2(g) + H2O(l) ⇌ H2SO3(aq) describes that aqueous acid system. Its reverse direction and changing concentrations matter, so it is not a claim that the liquid contains only one isolated molecular species.

Across the selected oxides, strongly basic behaviour gives way through amphoteric aluminium oxide to acidic non-metal oxides. Acidic-oxide character does not imply ready dissolution in water: SiO2 is an acidic oxide that does not simply form an acid solution with water, so reaction evidence must be interpreted separately from solubility. Use equations and named observations together to explain what each oxide does.

### Basic, acidic and amphoteric behaviour

Basic oxides react with acids to form a salt and water. For example, MgO(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl2(aq) + H2O(l). Magnesium hydroxide behaves similarly: Mg(OH)2(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl2(aq) + 2H2O(l). Sodium hydroxide neutralises an acid through H+(aq) + OH−(aq) → H2O(l). Its high water solubility is a separate property from its ability to accept protons.

Aluminium oxide and aluminium hydroxide are amphoteric: they react with acids and with strong alkali such as sodium hydroxide. In acid, Al2O3(s) + 6H+(aq) → 2Al3+(aq) + 3H2O(l). In aqueous alkali, Al2O3(s) + 2OH−(aq) + 3H2O(l) → 2[Al(OH)4]−(aq). The hydroxide analogues are Al(OH)3(s) + 3H+(aq) → Al3+(aq) + 3H2O(l), and Al(OH)3(s) + OH−(aq) → [Al(OH)4]−(aq).

The hydroxoaluminate notation states the aqueous alkaline product. If a problem specifies a different heated or dehydrated product form, balance the equation for that stated form instead. Do not mix an aqueous complex product and an anhydrous salt representation without accounting for water. Sodium ions can be omitted as spectators in the net ionic version.

An acidic oxide reacts with alkali. For example, SO3 + 2NaOH(aq) → Na2SO4(aq) + H2O(l), and heated SiO2(s) + 2NaOH → Na2SiO3 + H2O. The latter needs suitable strong-alkali heating and is not a claim of rapid reaction with a dilute cold solution. For phosphorus(V) oxide, full neutralisation gives P4O10 + 12NaOH → 4Na3PO4 + 6H2O; the stated amount of base determines the degree of neutralisation. Explain amphoterism by both acid and alkali reactions, rather than merely saying that a substance has an intermediate pH.

### Chlorides with water: dissolving or reacting

Sodium chloride dissolves by separating and hydrating its ions. It does not undergo substantial acid-producing hydrolysis, so a simple aqueous NaCl solution is approximately neutral. Magnesium chloride also supplies hydrated ions and is commonly described as weakly acidic rather than as violently hydrolysing. The magnesium cation's interaction with surrounding water is different from sodium's.

Aluminium chloride gives a distinctly acidic aqueous solution. Although the anhydrous chloride has covalent character and the syllabus uses the Al2Cl6 dimer description, water forms hydrated aluminium ions. A hydrated Al3+ ion strongly polarises O–H bonds in attached water, allowing proton transfer to surrounding water. A useful first-stage representation is [Al(H2O)6]3+(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ [Al(H2O)5OH]2+(aq) + H3O+(aq). The increased H3O+ concentration explains acidity. Do not assume that simply adding much water precipitates all aluminium as Al(OH)3.

Silicon tetrachloride reacts strongly with water: SiCl4(l) + 2H2O(l) → SiO2(s) + 4HCl(aq). The white solid is often hydrated silica in practice, and hydrogen chloride produces acidic fumes in moist air. The simplified equation accounts for the main composition without representing the real solid as a single dissolved ion.

With excess water, PCl5(s) + 4H2O(l) → H3PO4(aq) + 5HCl(aq). With limited water other intermediate products can be retained, so the excess-water qualification belongs to this equation. The gaseous molecular description of PCl5 must also be distinguished from its ionic solid structure when interpreting physical data. Across these examples, soluble ionic chlorides and hydrolysing covalent chlorides can both produce conducting solutions; the solution products, rather than the original bonding alone, carry charge. Distinguish dissolution from hydrolysis by whether a chemical reaction with water produces new species such as acid.

### Interpreting the pattern through bonding

Sodium and magnesium are electropositive metals. Their large electronegativity differences from oxygen or chlorine favour ionic descriptions for the usual oxides and chlorides. Across Period 3, electronegativity generally increases. The difference from oxygen or chlorine becomes smaller, and shared-electron covalent descriptions become more important. Aluminium sits in a useful intermediate position: its oxide is commonly treated as an ionic lattice with appreciable covalent character, while its anhydrous chloride has a strongly covalent description.

Silicon dioxide is a giant covalent network, whereas SiCl4 is molecular. Both contain silicon formally at +4, so oxidation number alone does not decide whether the compound is molecular, giant or ionic. The partners, geometry and bonding arrangement matter. Phosphorus and sulphur oxides and their reactions with water provide further examples of covalent non-metal chemistry.

The acid/base trend is related but needs its own evidence. Basic Na2O and MgO react with acids; Al2O3 reacts with acid and alkali; selected non-metal oxides react with alkali and often form acidic solutions with water. SiO2 requires particular care because its strong network resists ordinary water reaction despite its acidic-oxide behaviour. A decreasing water-reaction rate is not the same as a decreasing tendency to act as an acid towards alkali.

When interpreting a supplied table, connect a property to the interaction that explains it. A low boiling point can support a molecular structure with weak intermolecular forces. A high melting point may instead indicate an ionic lattice or a covalent network, which further evidence must distinguish. Acidity after adding water describes the products of that interaction, not a direct measurement of the original compound's bond type. Use several linked observations to support the periodic interpretation.

### Inferring bonding from a set of observations

Bonding inference is an argument from evidence rather than a name attached to one property. A chloride that has a high melting point, does not conduct as a solid and conducts when molten is consistent with an ionic lattice. Fixed ions explain the solid's lack of conduction, and mobile ions explain the melt. The high melting point reflects strong lattice attractions.

A volatile chloride with a low boiling point and poor electrical conduction as a pure liquid is consistent with discrete molecules. Weak intermolecular attractions allow easy separation of the molecules. Its internal covalent bonds need not be weak. If adding water produces an acidic conducting solution, the new solution may contain ions formed by hydrolysis; that does not retrospectively prove the original liquid was ionic.

A high-melting oxide that is a poor ordinary conductor can be a giant covalent network such as SiO2. High melting point alone cannot distinguish it from MgO. Look for molten conduction, reaction behaviour or other stated evidence before choosing a structure. Likewise, a semiconducting element should not be treated as a typical metal merely because a small current can pass.

Consider two invented observations: chloride A melts at a high temperature and conducts only after melting; chloride B is a volatile nonconducting liquid that forms acid with water. Ionic A and molecular B are supported interpretations, but the measurements do not identify their elements uniquely. Use the Period 3 possibilities and any additional composition data to narrow identity. A good answer quotes the discriminating observation, supplies the particle model and states any remaining ambiguity. This is the same structure–property reasoning as Topic 1.3, now used to make a deduction from unfamiliar chloride and oxide evidence.

---

## The Periodic Table and chemical periodicity — 3.1.4

### Making a controlled group prediction

An element's group provides a useful first prediction because main-group members share a related outer-electron arrangement. Group 2 atoms have two outer electrons and commonly form 2+ ions. Group 17 atoms have seven outer electrons and commonly form 1− halide ions in ionic salts. Group similarity predicts a family of behaviour, not identical numerical properties.

Use a known neighbour as a comparison. For a Group 2 element below magnesium, larger radius and greater shielding make removal of outer electrons easier in the general trend. Stronger reaction with water may therefore be expected when comparing otherwise suitable samples. It is not necessary to invent an exact time or gas-production rate. Surface oxide, temperature and physical form can affect observations, so state the qualitative basis of the prediction.

For a Group 17 element below chlorine, predict larger atoms and halide ions, and lower electronegativity. Its elemental form remains diatomic in the ordinary halogen pattern. Avoid transferring the metal's electron-loss reactivity explanation directly to a halogen's electron-gain chemistry. The shared periodic vocabulary of charge, radius and shielding does not make their chemical roles the same.

When asked to suggest a property of an unfamiliar element, start with the stated group and the relevant comparison. Link the predicted property to an outer-electron or structural reason. Distinguish a direct group feature, such as typical ion charge, from a down-group tendency, such as changing radius. If the group is not given, use composition, ionisation or reaction data first to infer it. An uncertain position should give a conditional prediction rather than a falsely certain identity. The following section combines those clues to identify an unknown.

### Combining clues to identify an unknown

An unknown element is best identified from several independent clues. Electrical conduction and metallic appearance may indicate a metal but do not distinguish sodium, magnesium and aluminium. A typical ion charge can narrow the group. A known period or occupied-shell count then narrows the position further. Check that the proposed identity accounts for the chemical reactions as well as the physical evidence.

For an original example, an unknown is in Period 3, conducts as a solid, forms a common 2+ ion and gives a basic oxide. These clues together support magnesium. A metal below it in the same group would have more occupied shells and a larger atom, so it would not satisfy the Period 3 clue. A common 3+ ion would instead require a different candidate and acid/base evidence would need checking.

Successive ionisation data can provide another route. A large jump after the second electron has been removed suggests two relatively accessible outer electrons before reaching a more tightly held inner shell. Combined with a Period 3 location and metallic behaviour, that again supports Group 2 magnesium. The jump is evidence about electronic arrangement, not an instruction to use the largest raw number as a group label.

For a nonconducting Period 3 substance with a very high melting point, a giant covalent description suggests silicon rather than the simple molecular elements. If its chloride is a volatile liquid that hydrolyses, that strengthens the identification. Each extra clue should discriminate between candidates. Where the evidence leaves two plausible choices, name the uncertainty and state what further observation would decide. This is a chemical deduction: properties and electron arrangement must agree, rather than a guess from one familiar reaction.

1	# 3.2 Group 2
2	
3	*nam-8224-nsscas-2026. Offline study notes, rendered from the approved content units on 2026-10-22. Everything here is also what the flashcards are built from.*
4	
5	---
6	
7	## Group 2 — 3.2.1
8	
9	### Physical properties and the limits of a trend
10	
11	Group 2 contains beryllium, magnesium, calcium, strontium and barium among the familiar non-radioactive members. They are metals with two outer electrons and commonly form 2+ ions. Metallic bonding supplies cohesion, and delocalised electrons explain ordinary electrical and thermal conduction. A metallic appearance or conductivity alone does not identify which member is present.
12	
13	Down the group, atomic radius and the radius of comparable 2+ ions generally increase as occupied shells are added. First ionisation energy generally decreases because outer electrons are farther from the nucleus and more shielded. These electronic trends were established in Topic 3.1. Increased nuclear charge is present but does not reverse the additional-shell effect in the general ionisation comparison.
14	
15	Melting points do not follow a smooth one-way sequence. The general fall from the very high value for beryllium has departures, including calcium melting at a higher temperature than magnesium. Metallic attraction depends on ion size and the delocalised electron population, while different solid arrangements also matter. An explanation based only on steadily increasing radius cannot justify ignoring an observed rise in a supplied table.
16	
17	When describing physical-property data, distinguish a broad tendency from the actual neighbouring comparisons. If the question gives two measured melting points, quote the higher and lower correctly before relating them to a pattern. A numerical trend is evidence to interpret, not a line to overwrite with a memorised rule. Do not infer that the member with the lowest melting point must be the most reactive in water: melting and electron-loss reaction rates are different properties. Use radius and shielding for the reactivity argument, and structure for melting behaviour.
18	
19	### Reactions of the metals
20	
21	For a Group 2 metal M forming its simple oxide, 2M + O2 → 2MO. Magnesium gives the familiar bright white light on burning and a white magnesium oxide product. In air, other products can also form, so a simple oxygen equation describes the named oxide rather than guaranteeing a pure product from an open-air burn. The metal loses electrons and oxygen is reduced.
22	
23	Calcium, strontium and barium react with cold water to give the hydroxide and hydrogen: M(s) + 2H2O(l) → M(OH)2 + H2(g). The hydroxide's dissolved amount depends on its solubility and the water quantity. Calcium can give a cloudy mixture when solid calcium hydroxide is present. Reaction generally becomes more vigorous down this sequence as removal of outer electrons becomes easier.
24	
25	Magnesium is much slower with cold water, partly because its surface layer affects access. The cold-water product is Mg(OH)2, whereas heated magnesium with steam gives MgO(s) + H2(g). Beryllium does not show the same ready cold-water behaviour. State the member and water temperature rather than applying the most vigorous example to the whole group.
26	
27	With dilute hydrochloric acid, M(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MCl2(aq) + H2(g) for the usual reactive Group 2 examples. Effervescence accompanies gas formation and the metal is consumed. Use a suitable non-oxidising dilute acid for this simple hydrogen account; acid identity can alter the products. Dilute sulphuric acid can form a low-solubility sulphate coating on some lower members, reducing further reaction. Observed vigour therefore depends on both intrinsic electron-loss tendency and the surface/solution setting. Keep surface area and acid concentration comparable when testing a group trend.
28	
29	### Oxides, hydroxides and carbonates
30	
31	The oxide and hydroxide of a typical Group 2 metal show basic behaviour. Calcium oxide reacts with water to form calcium hydroxide, while magnesium oxide reacts much less readily and forms sparingly soluble magnesium hydroxide. An insoluble or sparingly soluble solid can still react with acid: the acid consumes basic species at the solid surface and in solution.
32	
33	The acid reaction of an oxide is MO(s) + 2H+(aq) → M2+(aq) + H2O(l). For a hydroxide, M(OH)2(s) + 2H+(aq) → M2+(aq) + 2H2O(l). With hydrochloric acid the corresponding chloride remains in the products. These are acid–base reactions; they do not produce hydrogen simply because the compound contains a metal. The metal in the oxide is already in its positive oxidation state.
34	
35	Carbonates are generally low-solubility solids and do not simply turn into hydroxide on adding ordinary water. With dilute acid, MCO3(s) + 2H+(aq) → M2+(aq) + CO2(g) + H2O(l). Effervescence is therefore expected. Carbon dioxide turns limewater milky under the appropriate test, whereas hydrogen from a metal–acid reaction has a different identity. Distinguish metal, oxide and carbonate before deciding which gas, if any, forms.
36	
37	As an original amount example, 0.0250 mol of calcium carbonate needs 0.0500 mol H+ for complete neutralisation and can produce 0.0250 mol CO2. The one-to-two acid ratio follows the balanced ionic equation. A carbonate may remain if acid is insufficient, so unchanged solid does not prove it cannot react. Compare acid amount, concentration, surface area and any product coating before attributing a slow observation to one cause. This prepares the agricultural neutralisation explanation later in the topic.
38	
39	### Heating carbonates and nitrates
40	
41	Thermal decomposition uses heat to break a compound into simpler products. A Group 2 carbonate forms the oxide and carbon dioxide on sufficient heating: MCO3(s) → MO(s) + CO2(g). For calcium carbonate this is the lime-making change, CaCO3(s) → CaO(s) + CO2(g). Carbon dioxide loss reduces the mass remaining in the heated container.
42	
43	For the Group 2 nitrates, the school decomposition pattern is 2M(NO3)2 → 2MO + 4NO2 + O2 on heating. Nitrogen dioxide gives brown fumes and oxygen is also produced. Do not write the carbonate products for a nitrate, or treat nitrogen dioxide's brown appearance as the identity of both gases. The gas amounts follow the coefficients: four moles of NO2 accompany one mole O2 in this equation. Check the oxygen balance explicitly: two M(NO3)2 units supply twelve oxygen atoms. Two remain in the oxide, eight enter the four NO2 units and two form O2. The metal amount is conserved as well. This atom count rejects a proposed nitrate equation that omits oxygen or uses an unbalanced gas coefficient.
44	
45	Thermal stability generally increases down the group for these salts. A smaller 2+ cation has a higher charge density and more strongly polarises the large carbonate or nitrate anion, making decomposition easier in the qualitative model. Larger cations lower down distort the anion less, so stronger heating is needed. This explanation concerns anion distortion and stability rather than a claim that the nitrate ion's formal charge changes down the group.
46	
47	For original arithmetic, 10.0 g of pure CaCO3 with molar mass 100 g mol⁻¹ contains 0.100 mol. Complete heating yields 0.100 mol CaO, or 5.60 g using 56.0 g mol⁻¹, and 0.100 mol CO2. The mass decrease is 4.40 g. This assumes complete decomposition and no loss of solid. A short heating period may leave carbonate, giving a larger final residue than the complete-decomposition prediction. Topic 5.1 develops mass measurements and the use of repeated heating to assess completion.
48	
49	### Using a trend to make a prediction
50	
51	The word “reactive” needs a process. Group 2 metals generally react more readily down the group in the water comparison, while their carbonates generally resist thermal decomposition more strongly. These trends are not contradictory. One concerns electron removal from metal atoms; the other concerns stability of a compound containing M2+ and a large anion.
52	
53	For a metal below calcium, predict easier outer-electron removal from its larger, more shielded atom and generally more vigorous cold-water reaction. For its carbonate, predict greater thermal stability because the larger cation has lower polarising power. Do not carry one trend's arrow directly into the other explanation.
54	
55	Physical observations can give further evidence, but should be kept distinct. Metallic conductivity is a shared feature; irregular melting points need their own structural interpretation. If a supplied table shows a local rise, describe that rise rather than replacing it by the broad downward tendency. Solubility of hydroxides and sulphates also changes in opposite general directions, so “more soluble down the group” is incomplete without naming the compound family.
56	
57	When interpreting an experiment, check that the measurements compare the same temperature, acid concentration, water amount, surface condition and reaction time where these matter. A sulphate coating may slow metal–acid reaction even for a metal expected to lose electrons readily. An incomplete thermal decomposition may reflect insufficient heating rather than an incorrect final-product equation. Make the prediction from the appropriate chemical model, then identify the experimental limitation before drawing a stronger conclusion. This reasoning applies the attraction, shielding and bonding ideas from Topics 3.1 and 1.3 to unfamiliar group members without inventing exact numerical results.
58	
59	### Opposite solubility trends
60	
61	The hydroxides and sulphates show opposite general solubility trends down Group 2. Hydroxides become more soluble from magnesium towards barium, whereas sulphates become less soluble. State the compound family in the answer. A group-position prediction without naming hydroxide or sulphate can give the wrong result.
62	
63	Magnesium hydroxide is sparingly soluble. Calcium hydroxide has limited solubility but supplies enough dissolved hydroxide to give alkaline limewater. The lower Group 2 hydroxides dissolve more readily in the general trend. More dissolved hydroxide in a saturated solution can give greater alkalinity, but compare at the same temperature and recognise that adding extra solid beyond saturation does not simply keep increasing the dissolved concentration.
64	
65	Magnesium sulphate is readily soluble, while barium sulphate is very low-solubility. Calcium sulphate is much less soluble than magnesium sulphate. Precipitation depends on the concentrations of the ions mixed, so a very dilute solution can fail to give a visible solid even when a salt is described as low-solubility. Conversely, a precipitate is an observation about a particular mixture, not a measurement of an element's metallic reactivity.
66	
67	For a qualitative prediction between calcium and barium, expect the barium hydroxide to be more soluble but the barium sulphate to be less soluble under comparable aqueous settings. Solubility reflects the balance between separating a lattice and stabilising ions in water; changing cation size influences those contributions differently for the two anions. The syllabus requires the observed directions and their use in predictions, rather than a numerical dissolution calculation. Keep the trends separate from acid reactions: low-solubility magnesium hydroxide can still neutralise acid, and a sulphate coating can influence how much metal remains accessible.
68	
69	---
70	
71	## Group 2 — 3.2.2
72	
73	### Slaking lime
